name: Under-eye cooling mask
lead: An under-eye cooling mask is a reusable gel or cold-pack patch worn over the lower eyelids and cheeks for a few minutes, typically after sleep or a late night, to reduce the look of puffy eyes and give a more rested, defined eye area. It is a form of local cryotherapy, the therapeutic use of low temperatures, which is more widely used for sprains, muscle soreness and swelling after surgery or soft tissue injury.[1]

Cooling the skin is described as narrowing blood vessels and reducing blood flow to swollen tissue.[1] Cold compresses are a long-standing home approach to periorbital puffiness: Wikipedia lists a cold compress as a short-term remedy that constricts vessels and reduces fluid leaking into the tissue, and Cleveland Clinic lists chilled washcloths, wrapped ice packs, cucumber slices, chilled tea bags and cold spoons among home options.[6][7] Gel masks are a packaged, reusable version of the same routine.

Research specific to cooling masks comes mainly from surgery. A 2024 randomized trial after rhinoplasty found that a cooling gel eye mask was associated with lower pain and swelling scores than ice in a latex glove,[2] and a 2025 pilot study of 23 patients reported that a temperature-controlled periocular mask reduced eyelid swelling for the first day after upper blepharoplasty.[3] No published trial appears to have tested cooling masks for everyday morning puffiness in otherwise healthy people. Cold exposure has documented limits, including contraindications in people with cold allergy or cold-induced urticaria, and rare cold injury with prolonged or intense cooling.[1][4]

paras: Cooling eye masks are usually soft gel-filled pads, sometimes shaped to sit over the lower lids and upper cheeks, that are stored in a refrigerator or freezer and then worn while resting. Some are strap-on masks that cover the whole eye area. They are a commercial version of the long-standing practice of placing a cold compress or chilled objects on the eyes.

Periorbital puffiness is swelling of the tissue around the eyes, usually from fluid build-up (periorbital edema), and mild swelling just below the eyes is often called eye bags. Wikipedia lists many contributors: aging, which thins skin and enlarges the fat pad below the lower lid, allergy (described as the most common cause), crying, sleep loss, high salt intake, alcohol and tobacco, hormonal conditions and infections.[6] Cleveland Clinic adds that some eye bags are genetic, related to fat pad prominence, bone structure or skin laxity, and that swelling lasting more than 24 to 48 hours should be seen by an eye care professional.[7]

Because morning puffiness is linked to fluid shifting while lying flat, Wikipedia and Cleveland Clinic both mention head elevation during sleep, and Cleveland Clinic mentions limiting salt and sleeping seven to nine hours as lifestyle measures alongside cold compresses.[6][7] Home-care and medical options listed by Cleveland Clinic for persistent bags include caffeine or retinol eye creams, dermal fillers, laser resurfacing, chemical peels and lower-lid blepharoplasty.[7]

Wikipedia credits James Arnott (1797 to 1883), a physician at Brighton Infirmary, with early therapeutic use of crushed ice and salt on tumors to reduce pain and inflammation. Whole-body cryotherapy chambers were built in Japan in the late 1970s following the work of rheumatologist Toshima Yamaguchi, and spread to Europe, the US and Australia in the 1980s and 1990s.[1] Eye masks are a consumer descendant of local cold packs rather than of these chambers.

Cryotherapy lowers tissue temperature and narrows the blood vessels, which reduces blood flow to the cooled area. Reference summaries describe this vasoconstriction as the basis for using cold to limit swelling after injury or surgery.[1]

A small laboratory study in six healthy adults, in which a cryotherapy unit cooled the knee for an hour, found that skin blood flow fell sharply during cooling and remained reduced for two hours of rewarming, even though skin temperature had largely recovered. The authors described this as persistent vasoconstriction and suggested it might contribute to non-freezing cold injury in some settings.[4] That study did not examine the eyelids or cosmetic masks.
No published clinical trial has evaluated an under-eye cooling mask for ordinary morning puffiness or under-eye bags in the general population. Evidence from related settings is as follows.

A 2024 randomized clinical trial published in Plastic and Aesthetic Nursing compared ice placed in disposable latex gloves with a cooling gel eye mask in patients after rhinoplasty. Outcomes included eye bruising, periorbital and facial swelling, pain and comfort. On the first postoperative day the ice-glove group had higher scores for pain around the eyes, facial pain and periorbital edema, and higher facial edema scores in the first hour. Patients using the gel mask reported sleeping more comfortably. The authors concluded that cooling gel eye masks reduced pain and swelling after rhinoplasty.[2]

A prospective pilot study published in Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery in 2025 (Liu and colleagues, University of Cologne) enrolled 23 patients (46 eyes) after upper blepharoplasty. One randomly assigned eye received one hour of Hilotherapy, a temperature-controlled water-circulating periocular mask set to 17 degrees C, and the other served as an untreated control; swelling was measured by 3D stereophotography. Eyelid area was smaller in treated eyes immediately afterwards (0.880 vs 1.129 square cm) and at 24 hours (1.146 vs 1.399 square cm), but the difference was no longer significant at two weeks. Positive response rates were about 70 percent at the end of treatment and 65 percent at 24 hours. The authors noted limitations including the small single-centre sample, no conventional cold-pack comparator and the lack of patient-reported outcomes, and said the colder setting had been poorly tolerated in preliminary testing.[3]

Wikipedia notes that ice-pack therapy is widely used and generally agreed to ease symptoms, but that testing has produced conflicting results about its effectiveness, and that some researchers have questioned whether icing after injury is helpful or may delay healing.[1] Systematic reviews of cryotherapy after knee replacement are described as inconclusive.[1] These findings concern injuries and surgery rather than cosmetic eye puffiness.

Contraindications listed for cryotherapy include cold allergy and conditions made worse by cold exposure such as urticaria and Raynaud syndrome, as well as impaired circulation or sensation in the treated area.[1] Frostbite and cold injury are associated with intense or prolonged cooling,[1][4] which is why products are usually designed for short applications at refrigerator rather than freezer-burn temperatures. The skin around the eyes is thin, and published surgical protocols use moderate temperatures; the pilot blepharoplasty study chose 17 degrees C because a 15 degrees C setting was poorly tolerated in preliminary testing.[3]

Puffiness has several possible causes, including fluid retention, allergy, fat prolapse and medical conditions, and a cooling mask is not designed to treat the underlying cause of persistent swelling. No trial has examined how long any cosmetic effect lasts.

Cooling masks and similar cold-compress routines are a common low-cost part of morning skincare and appear in appearance-focused discussions as a quick way to look less tired. The mechanism that proponents cite is vasoconstriction and reduced fluid pooling, in line with the physiology described in cryotherapy references.[1]

Products differ in whether they are gel pads or strap-on masks, whether they are intended for refrigerator or freezer storage, and in the thickness of the cloth barrier between gel and skin. Manufacturer instructions generally advise limiting application time and avoiding direct contact with frozen gel, and the cryotherapy literature lists cold allergy as a contraindication.[1]

Beyond cold packs, eye-area routines discussed in skincare media include caffeine or retinol eye creams, sleeping with the head slightly raised, reducing salt, and, for structural bags, fillers or surgery.[7] An older small study of eyelid warming devices (infrared heaters) addresses a different goal, meibomian gland and dry-eye care, rather than puffiness.[8]

timeline.event: Physician James Arnott is credited in some accounts with early therapeutic use of salt-and-ice mixtures for pain and inflammation.[1]
Toshima Yamaguchi's rheumatology work and the first whole-body cryotherapy chamber in Japan help popularize cold therapy.[1]
Aiache and Ramirez describe the lower-lid fat pad that enlarges with age, cited in Wikipedia's puffy eyes article.[6]
Laboratory study reports persistent reduction in skin blood flow after cutaneous cooling in healthy adults.[4]
Randomized trial reports a cooling gel eye mask was associated with less swelling and pain than ice gloves after rhinoplasty.[2]
Pilot study reports reduced eyelid swelling with a cooled periocular mask after blepharoplasty.[3]

lore.intro: Cold-compress routines for puffy eyes are described in dermatology-adjacent home-care guides and in skincare media as a quick morning step; gel masks are the packaged version.[7]

claims.claim: A cold compress or gel mask reduces morning puffiness
claims.believers: Home-care guides say a cold compress constricts vessels and reduces swelling within minutes.[6][7]
claims.experts: Cold-based reduction of swelling has been measured after rhinoplasty and eyelid surgery, and no trial has tested it for everyday puffiness.[2][3]

claims.claim: Cucumber slices, chilled tea bags or cold spoons work like a mask
claims.believers: Cleveland Clinic lists these as home options for puffy eyes.[7]
claims.experts: No published trial compares them with gel masks; their effect is generally attributed to the cold.[7]

claims.claim: Any puffiness can be fixed by cooling
claims.believers: Some users treat a cold mask as the main fix for tired-looking eyes.[7]
claims.experts: Clinicians note that eye bags can be genetic or due to fat pad prominence, bone structure or skin laxity, and that lasting swelling needs evaluation.[7]

claims.believers: Frozen packs are sometimes applied directly for a stronger effect.[7]
claims.experts: Sources advise a cloth barrier, and the blepharoplasty pilot chose 17 degrees C because a colder setting was poorly tolerated; prolonged cooling is associated with cold injury.[3][4][7]
